lessons.title: The Carbon Loop
lessons.mainIdea: Photosynthesis and respiration pass the same carbon atoms back and forth, and the whole planet breathes in a yearly rhythm.
reading: Put the two processes side by side. Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and water, stores energy, and releases oxygen. Respiration takes in oxygen and sugar, releases energy, and gives back carbon dioxide and water. The outputs of each are the inputs of the other. A carbon atom in a corn kernel in Illinois was in the air over that field in July. Eaten by a hog, it becomes part of a cell, is burned for energy, and returns to the air as carbon dioxide, ready for a leaf to catch it again next summer.

Plants do both. A leaf runs respiration all the time, day and night, in its mitochondria, because it needs ATP just as you do. In daylight, photosynthesis usually runs faster than respiration, so the leaf takes in more carbon than it gives off, and the plant gains mass. At night it only respires, and Ingenhousz was right that a plant in the dark spoils the air a little. Over a year, a growing forest is a net absorber of carbon. A forest that is rotting or burning is a net source.

You can see the planet doing this. Since 1958 a station on Mauna Loa in Hawaii has measured carbon dioxide in clean mid-Pacific air. The record shows a sawtooth. Every spring and summer, as the vast forests and fields of the Northern Hemisphere leaf out and photosynthesize, the number drops by several parts per million. Every autumn and winter, as leaves fall and rot and photosynthesis slows, it rises again. The Northern Hemisphere has most of Earth's land, so its growing season sets the rhythm. Earth inhales in May and exhales in October.

Under the sawtooth, the yearly average has climbed steadily, from about 317 parts per million in 1960 to over 400 today. That rise is not from respiration. It comes mostly from burning coal, oil and gas, which releases carbon that photosynthesis buried underground hundreds of millions of years ago, faster than today's plants and oceans can take it back up. Fossil fuel is ancient sunlight. Burning it is respiration on a planetary scale, without the matching photosynthesis.

lessons.title: The Cell Cycle
lessons.mainIdea: A cell grows, copies its DNA, checks its work, and only then divides, in a cycle that takes about a day for many human cells.
reading: You replace the entire lining of your gut about every week, and you replace your skin's outer layer about every month. Every second, your bone marrow releases millions of new red blood cells. All of that comes from cells dividing, and each division is the end of a repeating sequence called the *cell cycle*. A cell that divides on schedule keeps you alive. One that divides off schedule is the subject of a later lesson.

Most of the cycle is *interphase*, when the cell looks calm under a microscope but is working hard. In the first gap phase, G1, it grows, makes proteins and organelles, and decides whether conditions are right to continue. In the S phase, S for synthesis, it copies every one of its chromosomes so that there are two complete sets of DNA. In the second gap, G2, it grows more and checks the copies. Only then comes M phase, mitosis, when the two sets are pulled apart and the cell splits.

The cycle has *checkpoints*, moments when the cell pauses and takes stock. Is it big enough? Is there enough food? Is the DNA damaged? Was every chromosome copied exactly once? A protein called p53 is one of the inspectors; if it finds broken DNA it halts the cycle until repairs are made, or if the damage is too great, orders the cell to destroy itself. Checkpoints are why most damaged cells never become tumors. They are the quality control of the body.

Different cells run the cycle at different speeds. Human cells growing in a lab dish take about 24 hours to go around once. Cells lining the gut divide faster. Mature nerve and heart muscle cells mostly leave the cycle altogether and never divide again, which is why damage to the brain or heart heals so poorly. Liver cells sit quietly for years but can re-enter the cycle when the liver is injured, which is why a liver can regrow much of itself after surgery.

lessons.title: Mitosis, Step by Step
lessons.mainIdea: Mitosis sorts two identical sets of chromosomes into two nuclei, and cytokinesis then splits the cell in two.
reading: In the 1880s the German anatomist Walther Flemming stained salamander cells with dyes and saw threads inside the nucleus thicken, line up, and pull apart in the dividing cell. He named the process *mitosis*, from the Greek for thread. The threads were chromosomes, though he did not know they carried genes. Under the microscope today, with a stain and a 400x objective, a root tip of an onion shows every stage he drew.

Before mitosis begins, S phase has already copied each chromosome. The two copies, called sister chromatids, stay attached at one point. The first stage is prophase. The loose DNA coils tightly into short, visible chromosomes. The membrane around the nucleus breaks down. A scaffold of protein fibers, the *spindle*, forms between the two ends of the cell. In metaphase, spindle fibers attach to each chromosome. They line all of them up along the middle of the cell, like players at a center line.

In anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled apart, one copy toward each end of the cell. This is the moment that matters: each end now has a complete, identical set. In telophase the chromosomes uncoil, and a new nuclear membrane forms around each set. Finally, *cytokinesis* divides the cytoplasm. An animal cell pinches in at the middle until it splits. A plant cell, with its stiff wall, instead builds a new wall down the center. The result is two cells, each with the same 46 chromosomes as the original, for a human.

Mitosis is copying, not mixing. The daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent, which is exactly what you want when replacing skin, healing a cut or growing from a fertilized egg to an adult. This is Virchow's rule in action. A different kind of division, meiosis, makes sperm and egg cells with half the chromosomes each; it shuffles genes, and it belongs to the study of heredity.

the two identical copies of a chromosome, joined together until anaphase

look.title: All Cells from Cells
look.text: Virchow insisted that where a cell arises, a cell must have existed before it, just as an animal comes only from an animal and a plant only from a plant. He rejected the older belief that cells could crystallize out of a formless fluid, and summed up his position in three Latin words: omnis cellula e cellula, every cell from a cell.
look.cite: Rudolf Virchow, lectures on cellular pathology, Berlin, 1855 to 1858
look.prompt: If every cell comes from a cell, then every cell in your body traces back through an unbroken chain of divisions. How far back does that chain go?

check.q: What happens during anaphase?
choices: Sister chromatids are pulled apart toward opposite ends of the cell
The DNA is copied
The nuclear membrane re-forms
The cell pinches into two
check.why: Anaphase is the separation step. Each end of the cell receives one complete set of chromosomes.

check.q: How do the two cells produced by mitosis compare to the original cell?
choices: Each has half the chromosomes
Each has the same chromosomes as the original
Each has twice the chromosomes
They have different, shuffled sets of chromosomes
check.why: Mitosis distributes two identical copies. Meiosis, a different process, halves and shuffles them.

check.q: Why does a plant cell finish dividing differently from an animal cell?
choices: Plant cells do not have a spindle
Plant cells copy DNA after mitosis
A plant cell has a rigid wall and cannot pinch in, so it builds a new wall down the middle
Plant cells have no cytoplasm
check.why: Cytokinesis in animals is a pinch. In plants it is a new wall laid across the center of the cell.

lessons.title: When Division Goes Wrong
lessons.mainIdea: Cancer is the result of damage to the genes that control the cell cycle, so cells divide without limit and spread.
reading: Every day, some of your cells suffer damage to their DNA, from sunlight, from chemicals, from ordinary copying mistakes. Nearly all of it is repaired or the damaged cell destroys itself at a checkpoint. But a few genes are the control system itself: genes that step on the gas of the cell cycle and genes that hit the brakes. If a cell collects mutations that jam the gas and cut the brakes, it divides when it should not, and its daughters do too. That is *cancer*. It is not one disease but hundreds, and each one begins as a cell breaking the rules of the cycle.

A clump of runaway cells is a *tumor*. If the cells stay in one place and keep their neighbors' boundaries, the tumor is benign and can usually be removed. A *malignant* tumor is one whose cells invade nearby tissue and, worst of all, travel through the blood or lymph to start new tumors elsewhere, a process called *metastasis*. Cancer cells also ignore the signals that tell normal cells to stop, evade the immune system, and grow new blood vessels to feed themselves. They are the body's own cells, following broken instructions.

What damages the control genes? Tobacco smoke is the largest preventable cause; its chemicals mutate DNA in the lungs, mouth and bladder. Ultraviolet light from the sun damages skin cell DNA. Some viruses insert their genes into ours; the human papillomavirus causes most cervical cancer, which is why there is now a vaccine against it. Some people inherit a faulty brake gene and start with one strike already. And time itself matters: the older a cell line, the more mutations it has had a chance to collect, which is why most cancers appear later in life.

Because cancer is division gone wrong, most treatments attack dividing cells. Radiation and many chemotherapy drugs damage DNA or break the spindle, which hits fast-dividing cancer cells hardest but also hits hair follicles and the gut lining, causing the familiar side effects. Newer drugs target the specific broken proteins in a patient's tumor. Much of what we know came from a single line of cells, taken in 1951 from a Baltimore woman named Henrietta Lacks, which has divided in labs around the world ever since. Her story also forced hard questions about consent that medicine is still answering.

words.d: a disease in which cells with damaged control genes divide without limit and may spread
a mass of cells produced by uncontrolled division
describing a tumor whose cells invade nearby tissue and can spread
the spread of cancer cells from the original tumor to other parts of the body
a change in the DNA sequence

look.title: What Cancer Is
look.text: The National Cancer Institute describes cancer as a disease in which some of the body's own cells grow out of control and spread to other parts of the body. It notes that cancer can begin almost anywhere in the trillions of cells of the human body, and that normally cells grow and divide to form new cells as the body needs them, dying when they are old or damaged and being replaced.
look.cite: U.S. National Cancer Institute, public information page on cancer, National Institutes of Health
look.prompt: The definition says cancer starts in the body's own cells. Why does that make it harder for the immune system to fight than an infection by bacteria?

check.q: What is the basic cause of cancer at the level of the cell?
choices: An infection by bacteria
A shortage of ATP
Cells losing their membranes
Mutations in the genes that control the cell cycle, so cells divide without limit
check.why: Cancer begins when the gas and brake genes of division are damaged. The cell keeps cycling when it should stop.

check.q: What makes a malignant tumor more dangerous than a benign one?
choices: Its cells invade nearby tissue and can spread to distant parts of the body
It grows faster in cold weather
It is always larger
It contains no DNA
check.why: Metastasis, the spread to new sites, is what makes cancer hard to remove and treat.

check.q: Why do many chemotherapy drugs cause hair loss?
choices: They are applied to the scalp
They attack rapidly dividing cells, and hair follicle cells divide rapidly too
Hair is made of cancer cells
They stop photosynthesis in the skin
check.why: Drugs aimed at dividing cells cannot tell a tumor cell from a fast-dividing normal cell in a hair follicle or the gut lining.

lessons.title: Stem Cells and Specialization
lessons.mainIdea: All your cells carry the same DNA; they differ because they read different genes, and stem cells are the ones that have not yet chosen.
reading: You began as one cell. Nine months later you were tens of trillions, of roughly 200 different kinds. The first cell divided by mitosis into two identical cells, then four, then eight. Somewhere along the way, cells that were identical began to differ. Some became muscle, some nerve, some blood, some bone. This narrowing of a cell's options is called *differentiation*. Once a cell has become a heart muscle cell, it and its descendants stay heart muscle.

Differentiation does not change the DNA. A nerve cell and a skin cell in the same person carry the same instructions. What differs is which genes are switched on. Signals from neighboring cells, from position in the embryo and from chemical gradients tell each cell which chapters of the DNA to read. A cell reading the muscle chapters fills with contracting proteins. A cell reading the blood chapters fills with hemoglobin and, in the case of a red blood cell, eventually throws away its nucleus.

A *stem cell* is a cell that has not finished choosing. It can divide to make more stem cells or produce cells that go on to specialize. The cells of a very early embryo are *pluripotent*: they can become any cell type of the body. Adult stem cells are more limited. The ones in your bone marrow can make any kind of blood cell, but not nerve or muscle. That is what a bone marrow transplant is: giving a patient whose blood-making stem cells were destroyed by disease or by cancer treatment a new supply from a donor.

In 2006, the Japanese scientist Shinya Yamanaka made a surprising discovery. Adding just four genes could turn an ordinary adult skin cell back into a pluripotent stem cell. He shared a Nobel Prize for it in 2012. These induced pluripotent stem cells let researchers grow a patient's own nerve or heart cells in a dish. There they can study a disease or test a drug. Growing whole replacement organs remains far harder than headlines suggest. But the basic finding stands. Specialization is a setting, not a permanent rewrite, and it can be reset.

words.d: the process by which a cell becomes a specialized type by switching certain genes on and off
a cell that can keep dividing and can produce specialized cells
able to become any of the body's cell types
a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for one protein or one trait

look.title: The Same Book, Different Chapters
look.text: Picture a library where every reader is handed the same thick book. One reader is told to read only the chapters on cooking, another only the chapters on carpentry, a third only on music. By the end of the year, each is an expert in something different, though the books on their desks are identical.
look.prompt: In this picture, what stands for the DNA, and what stands for the signals that tell a cell what to become? Where would a stem cell fit?

check.q: A muscle cell and a nerve cell from the same person have different shapes and jobs. What is the reason?
choices: They have different DNA
Muscle cells have more chromosomes
They switch on different genes and so build different proteins
Nerve cells have lost most of their genes
check.why: Differentiation is about gene use, not gene content. The instructions are the same; the reading differs.

check.q: What can a bone marrow stem cell do that a mature red blood cell cannot?
choices: Carry oxygen
Live in the blood
Fit through capillaries
Keep dividing and produce new blood cells of different kinds
check.why: Stem cells retain the ability to divide and to produce specialized descendants. A mature red blood cell has no nucleus and cannot divide.

check.q: Why was Yamanaka's 2006 discovery important?
choices: It showed that a specialized adult cell can be reset to a pluripotent state, so specialization is not permanent
It proved that all cells have different DNA
It made mitosis unnecessary
It showed stem cells only exist in embryos
check.why: Four added genes turned skin cells back into stem cells, a result that changed both the science and the ethics of stem cell research.

lessons.title: Systems Working Together
lessons.mainIdea: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems, and no system does its job alone.
reading: Take a single stride during a run and count what has to happen. Muscle cells in your leg burn ATP. To recharge it they need oxygen and glucose, delivered by blood. The blood is pushed by the heart and loaded with oxygen in the lungs. Breathing speeds up because sensors in the brain notice rising carbon dioxide. The glucose came from a meal, broken down in the gut and stored in the liver. Sweat glands dump heat. Kidneys adjust water and salt. One stride, and most of your body is involved.

Biologists describe this as levels of organization. Cells of the same type working together form a *tissue*, such as muscle tissue or nerve tissue. Several tissues combined into a structure with a job form an *organ*: the heart is muscle tissue, nerve tissue, connective tissue and a lining, all working together. Organs that cooperate on a larger task form an *organ system*. The heart, blood vessels and blood make up the circulatory system. The human body has about a dozen such systems.

The key idea is that systems interact. The circulatory system carries what the respiratory system takes in and what the digestive system absorbs. The nervous system and the hormones of the endocrine system coordinate the rest, using the feedback loops from the last chapter. The skeletal and muscular systems move the whole thing around. The excretory system, mainly the kidneys, cleans the blood that every other system has been dumping waste into. Damage one system and the others feel it: a failing heart leaves the kidneys short of blood, and failing kidneys let waste build up that poisons the heart.

Step back and the whole unit fits together. Water and carbon build molecules. Molecules build cells. Cells run on ATP made from sugar that came, through a plant, from sunlight. Cells divide by mitosis, specialize, and organize into tissues, organs and systems that keep the inner environment steady. Priestley's mint and Priestley's mouse were the two halves of one loop. You are the mouse's side of it, made of about 37 trillion cells, every one of them descended from a single cell by the process in this chapter.

words.d: a group of similar cells working together on one job
a structure made of several tissues that performs a specific function, such as the heart
a group of organs that work together on a larger task, such as circulation
the heart, blood vessels and blood, which carry materials throughout the body

look.title: One Missed Meal
look.text: A student skips breakfast and lunch, then plays a full soccer match after school. Late in the second half she feels shaky and dizzy and cannot think clearly. A teammate hands her a juice box, and within ten minutes she feels almost normal.
look.prompt: Trace what happened through at least three organ systems, from the empty stomach to the shaky legs and back. Which feedback loop from the last chapter was involved?

check.q: Which sequence correctly lists levels of organization from smallest to largest?
choices: Organ, tissue, cell, organ system
Cell, tissue, organ, organ system
Tissue, cell, organ system, organ
Organ system, organ, tissue, cell
check.why: Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, and organs make organ systems.

check.q: During a run, your breathing speeds up. Which two systems are most directly coordinating this?
choices: The skeletal and digestive systems
The excretory and skeletal systems
The nervous system sensing carbon dioxide and the respiratory system responding
The digestive and endocrine systems
check.why: Sensors in the brain detect rising carbon dioxide and signal the breathing muscles to work harder.

check.q: A patient's kidneys fail. Why do doctors worry about the heart as well?
choices: The kidneys pump blood to the heart
The heart is made of kidney tissue
Kidney failure stops the heart from beating instantly
Wastes the kidneys normally remove build up in the blood and harm the heart, because organ systems depend on each other
check.why: No system works alone. The blood the heart pumps is the blood the kidneys are supposed to clean.

review.q: What did Priestley's mint do to the air in the sealed jar, in modern terms?
choices: It took in carbon dioxide and released oxygen by photosynthesis
It absorbed the smoke from the candle
It cooled the air so the candle could burn
It released carbon dioxide for the mouse to breathe
review.why: The candle had used up oxygen; the plant restored it while consuming the carbon dioxide the candle had produced.

review.q: Which correctly states the overall inputs and outputs of photosynthesis?
choices: Glucose and oxygen in; carbon dioxide and water out
Carbon dioxide and water in; glucose and oxygen out
Oxygen and water in; glucose and carbon dioxide out
Glucose and water in; oxygen and carbon dioxide out
review.why: Plants take in carbon dioxide and water, use light energy, and produce glucose and oxygen.

review.q: Which stage of cellular respiration produces the most ATP, and where does it happen?
choices: Glycolysis, in the cytoplasm
Fermentation, in the cytoplasm
The electron transport chain, in the inner membrane of the mitochondrion
The Calvin cycle, in the stroma
review.why: The electron chain and the ATP-making enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane produce most of the roughly 30 ATP per glucose.

review.q: A cell has plenty of glucose but no oxygen. What can it do?
choices: Run full aerobic respiration anyway
Switch to photosynthesis
Stop making ATP entirely
Use fermentation to keep glycolysis going, yielding only 2 ATP per glucose
review.why: Fermentation frees the electron carriers so glycolysis can continue without oxygen, at a much lower yield.

review.q: The Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record rises and falls each year. What causes the yearly dip?
choices: Northern Hemisphere plants photosynthesizing during their growing season
Volcanic eruptions on Mauna Loa
Ice melting in the Arctic
Animals breathing less in summer
review.why: When the vast land areas of the Northern Hemisphere leaf out, net photosynthesis draws carbon dioxide down for several months.

review.q: Put these in the correct order for a dividing cell.
choices: Mitosis, then DNA copying, then growth
Growth, then DNA copying, then mitosis, then cytokinesis
Cytokinesis, then mitosis, then DNA copying
DNA copying, then cytokinesis, then mitosis
review.why: G1 growth comes first, S phase copies the DNA, mitosis separates the sets, and cytokinesis splits the cell.

review.q: What is a checkpoint, and why does its failure matter for cancer?
choices: A place where cells exchange nutrients; failure causes starvation
A membrane channel; failure lets water in
A pause in the cell cycle where damage is detected; failure lets damaged cells keep dividing
The point where chromosomes line up; failure stops mitosis
review.why: Checkpoints catch damaged DNA. When the genes running them are mutated, damaged cells escape and can become tumors.

review.q: A skin cell and a nerve cell in one person differ because:
choices: They inherited DNA from different parents
Nerve cells have lost the skin genes
Skin cells have extra chromosomes
They express different sets of the same genes
review.why: Differentiation switches genes on and off. Every body cell keeps the full set of instructions.
